description: Figure 3 presents a set of three pie charts—labeled “easy,” “medium,” and “hard”—that visualize the distribution of problem outcomes based on correctness under two experimental conditions: “with knowledge” (w/ knowledge) and “without knowledge” (w/o knowledge), using CoT and VERIFY-ALL methods. Each pie chart is segmented into four colored categories, as defined by the legend: teal for N+K+ (correct with and without knowledge), yellow for N−K+ (incorrect without knowledge, correct with knowledge), orange for N−K− (incorrect both with and without knowledge), and red for N+K− (correct without knowledge, incorrect with knowledge). In the “easy” chart, the largest segment is N+K+ at 61.5%, followed by N−K+ at 34.6%, N−K− at 3.1%, and N+K− at 0.8%. The “medium” chart shows N+K+ as the dominant segment at 65.4%, with N−K+ at 30.8%, N−K− at 2.5%, and N+K− at 1.3%. In the “hard” chart, N+K+ drops to 25.1%, N−K+ is 39.6%, N−K− is 30.6%, and N+K− is 4.7%. The chart visually emphasizes that for easy and medium problems, most errors are resolved with knowledge (N−K+), while for hard problems, a large proportion of errors persist even with knowledge (N−K−), indicating a bottleneck in geometric reasoning rather than knowledge access.
